title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: It was a wet day. Rain had been falling all morning, and the invalids, parasols up, had crowded into the arcades.

Kitty was walking there with her mother and the Moscow colonel — smart and jaunty in his European coat, picked up ready-made in Frankfurt. They kept to one side of the arcade, trying to avoid Levin, who was walking down the other. Varenka, in her dark dress and a black hat with a turned-down brim, paced the whole length of the arcade with a blind Frenchwoman, and each time she passed Kitty they exchanged friendly looks.
"Mamma, couldn't I speak to her?" Kitty said, watching her unknown friend and noticing that she was heading toward the spring, where they might reach it at the same time.

"Oh, if you want to so badly, let me find out about her first and make her acquaintance myself," her mother answered. "What is it you see in her? She must be a paid companion. If you like, I'll introduce myself to Madame Stahl — I used to know her _belle-sœur_," the princess added, lifting her head loftily.
Kitty knew that the princess had taken offense at the way Madame Stahl had seemed to avoid meeting her. Kitty did not press the point.
"How wonderfully sweet she is!" she said, watching Varenka just as she handed a glass to the Frenchwoman. "Look how natural it all is, how kind."

"Your _engouements_ are so funny to watch," said the princess. "No — let's turn back," she added, spotting Levin coming toward them with his companion and a German doctor, all three talking very loudly and angrily.

They were turning back when suddenly they heard, not talk, but shouting. Levin had stopped short and was yelling at the doctor, and the doctor was shouting too. A crowd was gathering. The princess and Kitty beat a hasty retreat, while the colonel pushed into the crowd to find out what had happened.
A few minutes later the colonel caught up with them.
"What happened?" the princess asked.

"A scandal — disgraceful!" the colonel answered. "The one thing one dreads abroad is running into Russians. That tall man was abusing the doctor, throwing every kind of insult at him because he wasn't treating him the way he wanted, and then he started waving his stick at him. It's simply a scandal!"
"Oh, how unpleasant!" said the princess. "And how did it end?"
"Luckily at that point that — the one in the mushroom hat — stepped in. A Russian lady, I think," said the colonel.
"Mademoiselle Varenka?" Kitty asked.
"Yes, yes. She came to the rescue before anyone else; she took the man by the arm and led him away."
"There, mamma," said Kitty. "You wonder that I'm so enthusiastic about her."

The next day, watching her unknown friend, Kitty saw that Mademoiselle Varenka was already on the same terms with Levin and his companion as with her other _protégés_. She went up to them, fell into conversation with them, and acted as interpreter for the woman, who could not speak a foreign language.

Kitty began begging her mother even more urgently to let her make friends with Varenka. And disagreeable as it was for the princess to seem to be the first to seek out Madame Stahl, who was apparently giving herself airs, she made inquiries about Varenka and, finding that the acquaintance could do no harm even if it did little good, she approached Varenka herself and introduced herself.
Choosing a moment when her daughter had gone off to the spring and Varenka had paused outside the baker's, the princess went up to her.
"Allow me to introduce myself," she said with her dignified smile. "My daughter has lost her heart to you," she said. "You may not know who I am. I am — "
"That feeling is more than mutual, princess," Varenka answered quickly.
"What a kind thing you did yesterday for our poor compatriot!" the princess said.
Varenka flushed a little. "I don't remember. I don't think I did anything," she said.
"Why, you saved that Levin from real trouble."
"Yes — _sa compagne_ called me over, and I tried to calm him down. He's very ill and was unhappy with the doctor. I'm used to looking after that kind of patient."
"Yes, I'd heard you live at Mentone with your aunt — I think — Madame Stahl. I used to know her _belle-sœur_."
"No, she isn't my aunt. I call her mamma, but I am not related to her; I was brought up by her," Varenka answered, coloring slightly again.
She said it so simply, and her face was so candid and truthful, that the princess saw at once why Kitty had taken such a fancy to Varenka.
"Well, and what is this Levin going to do?" the princess asked.
"He's leaving," Varenka answered.
At that moment Kitty came up from the spring, beaming because her mother had at last made her unknown friend's acquaintance.
"Well, you see, Kitty — your great desire to make friends with Mademoiselle —"
"Varenka," Varenka put in, smiling. "That's what everyone calls me."

Kitty blushed with pleasure and, slowly and silently, pressed her new friend's hand. The hand did not return the pressure but lay still in hers. Yet Mademoiselle Varenka's face lit up with a soft, glad, if rather sad smile that showed her large but handsome teeth.
"I have wanted this for a long time too," she said.
"But you're so busy."
"Oh, no — I'm not busy at all," Varenka answered, but at that very moment she had to leave her new friends: two little Russian girls, an invalid's children, came running up to her.
"Varenka, mamma's calling!" they cried.
And Varenka went off with them.
